title: SGD, Momentum & Adam
interviewAnswer: SGD follows noisy mini-batch gradients; momentum smooths updates by accumulating velocity; Adam adapts step sizes using first and second gradient moments. No optimizer is universally best.
why: SGD vs Momentum vs Adam tests whether you understand how parameter updates are constructed and why optimization behavior differs.
intuition: SGD follows the current noisy gradient. Momentum remembers recent directions to smooth oscillation. Adam additionally adapts the step scale per parameter using running gradient statistics.
deepDive: Momentum maintains an exponentially decayed velocity, accelerating consistent directions and damping zig-zag behavior. Adam tracks first and second moments of gradients with bias correction, often giving fast robust convergence. Weight decay should be understood carefully: AdamW decouples weight decay from Adam’s adaptive gradient step. Optimizer choice interacts with learning-rate schedule, batch size and generalization.
math:
Momentum: v_t=βv_{t-1}+g_t; θ←θ-ηv_t
Adam: m_t=β₁m_{t-1}+(1-β₁)g_t; v_t=β₂v_{t-1}+(1-β₂)g_t²; update with bias-corrected m/√v
workedExample: If SGD oscillates across a narrow valley, momentum can average those alternating directions while preserving movement along the valley.
commonMistakes: Saying Adam is universally better than SGD.
Confusing L2 regularization with decoupled AdamW weight decay.
Comparing optimizers without retuning learning rates/schedules.
followUps: Why can SGD generalize well in vision?
production: Log optimizer configuration and scheduler state with checkpoints. Changing optimizer/schedule can invalidate comparisons even when architecture and data are unchanged.
